# Cordilla account triage — impact, agent, monitoring

**A rep can work about 40 accounts a day out of tens of thousands. This picks which 40, tells them why
each one is on the list, and says plainly when the honest answer is "none of these yet, buy fresh data
first".**

The model needed for that already exists and does its job. What was missing is everything around it,
and that is where the risk sits: Cordilla has two scarce resources, rep hours and rep trust, and the
previous scoring effort spent the second to buy the first.

*Every figure is regenerated by `python analysis/profile.py` into `analysis/findings.json`.
Assumptions are labelled. 1,295 words of prose plus two tables.*

---

## 1 · What this is worth

**The decision.** An SDR picks tomorrow's ~40 calls from tens of thousands of accounts. Today that is
guesswork. After this the queue is chosen, ordered, bounded, and carries a reason the rep can read.

**What the model can do.** Split its training accounts into ten bands by score: the **highest-scoring
tenth converted at 26.7% against a 6.5% average, a 4.1x lift**. The next band manages 1.28x, and below
the fourth the ordering is no better than shuffling — the fifth band converts *worse* than the tenth.
It is a filter for the top slice, not a ranking to work down.

Two caveats before anyone gets excited:

- **The scores are not probabilities.** The top band predicts 13.9% and delivers 26.7%; the middle
  predicts 5.6% and delivers 0.8%. Multiplying a score by deal value would be wrong sevenfold in the
  middle of the range.
- **4.1x is a ceiling**, because it was measured on the very accounts the model learned from. The
  model also kept its own internal check while being built, on data withheld from each stage, and it
  is sobering: **19 of its 40 stages made results on withheld data worse**, the last ten net negative.

**What I would commit to.** Two routes agree on magnitude. The band-by-band table says up to 4.1x. The
brief's own rates (under 1% cold, low single digits for engaged accounts) imply 2-4x from shifting rep
time alone. **Plan on 2x**, half the ceiling, and let the holdout produce the real number.

In rep terms: **~15 calls per win** at the average rate, **~3.4** in the top band, again measured on
the accounts it learned from.

*Assumptions, benchmarked not invented:* 5 SDRs × 40 dials × 20 days ≈ 1,000 accounts monthly
(2026 bands: 40-50 dials/day, 50-150 prospects/rep/week, so we sit low), and **$15k ACV** against a
2026 median of $24k. At 1% that is ~10 wins; at 2x, ~20, worth roughly **$150k new ARR monthly**.
The ACV carries that last sentence, not the model. The claim I defend is calls-per-win.

**Do the gates help?** `analysis/policy_backtest.py` tests them against the 1,099 accounts whose
outcome is known. Not provably: freshness points the right way (21.4% against 31.5%) but the ranges of
uncertainty overlap. They stay on structural grounds, and closing that gap is what the control group
is for.

**Being wrong, each way.** A wasted call costs ~8 minutes; a missed account simply returns next run.
Arithmetic says over-include. **Rep trust says the opposite**, and trust is what the last effort lost,
so we protect precision at the cost of recall.

**The finding that reframes it.** **73% of the batch runs on information over 90 days old**, and every
feature is a 90-day window. So for **218 of 300 accounts the window being predicted has already
closed**. The model cannot see this; `snapshot_date` is not an input. Its top-scoring account was last
updated **October 2025**. Hand that to a rep and they reference a trial that ended ten months ago.

---

## 2 · The agent

A nightly batch job: validate → score → explain → route → write briefs → publish. The
model is used exactly as provided.

| Action | When | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `CALL_NOW` | ≥ 0.1088, data ≤ 90 days | The evidence bar — the training p90 |
| `CALL_WITH_CAVEAT` | same bar, 3–12 months old | Still top-decile; the brief states the age |
| `RE_ENRICH` | above the bar but over a year old, **or** the decision hinges on intent nobody measured | A refreshed record costs ~$1; a wasted call costs 8 minutes. On year-old data, buying the record is the cheaper experiment |
| `NURTURE` / `HOLD` | below the bar | Recorded with a reason — reps ask why |

Thresholds are **absolute**, from the training distribution, not "top 50 of today". A relative cut
absorbs a shift silently; an absolute one lets the tier overflow, and **that overflow is itself an
alarm**.

**Framework: LangGraph**, for four reasons: the batch can halt and that branch is visible; publishing
pauses for a human via `interrupt()`; the brief/verify retry is a real cycle rather than a loop hidden
in a helper; retries are declared per node. Honestly, though, stripped of the gate this is ~150 lines
of plain Python. **Scheduling is not LangGraph's job** — Airflow triggers the run, the graph decides
inside it.

**Where the LLM is allowed.** One node: the rep's brief. It returns sentences of `{{placeholders}}`
and no digits, code substitutes every value, and a verifier rejects any number it typed itself, falling
back to a template after two failures. No tools, no other accounts, no say in who gets called. Live on
`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` at **$0.019 a run, 0 rejections**.

**Why so little is autonomous.** Where to cut, what is too stale, who gets called: these must be
reproducible, explainable to a VP, and comparable against a control group. An LLM choosing them is none
of those. The exception is the ~20 accounts where the rule is arbitrary: they get a tool-calling loop
(`--investigate`) that decides what to check, with policy keeping veto. It changed 16 decisions, mostly
toward caution, and cost **$0.126 of the run's $0.138** — the argument for aiming it narrowly.

**Deployment.** Nightly against Salesforce, artifacts pinned by hash, records to a warehouse, rollback
on one flag. **Two weeks in shadow mode first**: score and record, publish nothing, compare against
what reps chose unaided.

## 3 · Monitoring

The failure that matters does not crash. `monitoring/demo_silent_failure.py` breaks the
real batch three ways and runs the real agent against each:

| Broken how | What the model reports | Checks |
|---|---|---|
| Intent coverage collapses | mean 0.0607, all valid | **RED — halted** |
| Refresh stalls (+200 days) | **mean 0.0655 — identical** | **RED — halted** |
| Upstream filter halves it | 105 accounts, all valid | **AMBER — paused** |

Zero exceptions in all three. The second is the point: ageing every snapshot by 200
days leaves the mean score **exactly** where it was.

**Three clocks.** *Daily:* intent coverage (40.2% training baseline, 38.7% today, ±5pp amber, ±10pp
red), staleness (median 121 days), batch size, score distribution. Needing no labels, these catch
things this week. *Four-weekly:* rep dispositions. *Quarterly:* conversion versus control.

**Problem versus noise.** At ~30 queued accounts weekly, one week's disposition rate
has a standard error of **7.3pp**, so 20% to 30% is noise. Over four weeks it falls to
**3.6pp**, where a 10pp shift is ~2.7 SE. That is the alert. Separating 15% conversion
from 6.5% at 80% power needs **~208 per arm**, about **14 weeks**. Alerting weekly on
conversion at a 6.5% base rate manufactures noise.

**Tracing.** LangSmith is wired and verified in two environment variables and no code. It replaces
neither `decisions.csv` nor the gate: the 90-day question is a join, not a trace, and our worst failure
produces a perfectly clean one.

**When it trips.** Red publishes nothing: a late queue costs a morning, a wrong one costs the
programme. Amber pauses for a named owner, and `monitoring/RUNBOOK.md` gives each alert a first move.

**Proving it works.** 30% of the call tier is held back each run, assigned by hashing the account ID
so none drifts between treated and control. Without that, nobody can separate "the model worked" from
"the quarter was good", so the run summary prints lift as **pending**, never estimated.

---

## 4 · What I would not claim

The 4.1x was measured on the accounts the model learned from. The per-account reasons come from
removing one fact at a time, so they miss facts that only matter in combination. Capacity and ACV are
assumptions. And **101 training rows younger than 90 days are all labelled "did not convert"** because
their window had not closed: harmless now, corrosive if anyone retrains on a rolling window.
